reading.body:
Maryland's 2026 legislative session treated AI as a consumer protection problem first and an infrastructure problem second, with 104 bills spanning chatbots, deepfakes, health care, schools, and data centers.

The largest cluster regulates what AI does to people rather than how it is built. Bills cover companion chatbots, AI toys, behavioral health prohibitions, insurance claim review, algorithmic rent setting, surveillance-based wage and price setting, facial recognition, and deepfake identity fraud. Data privacy and data broker registry bills appear repeatedly, often in House and Senate pairs, which suggests broad interest rather than a single sponsored effort.

A smaller but distinct group addresses the physical layer. Bills on data center siting, operation standards, planning and transparency, county property tax subclasses for data center equipment, a sales and property tax exemption repeal, a moratorium on new data center construction, and large load customer interconnection and demand response programs all point at the same tension: compute capacity, electricity supply, and local tax treatment. The Utility RELIEF Act appears twice. This is the only part of the data that touches power and buildings directly.

The data does not say which bills passed, which died, or what any of them require. It records titles, numbers, and dates, not outcomes or text. Three news items appear, one about a Seattle grocery pricing ban, one about Governor Moore outlining an AI framework, and one about governors generally, so the state-level picture here is legislative activity, not enacted law.
